From the Greek philos (love) and sophia (wisdom). Wisdom here means discernment (vivek), not memory. It is called the mother of all disciplines because every field began as a question humans asked when life troubled them.
The Indian word, from the root drish: to see. A philosopher sees something about the world and life that ordinary looking does not show.
The eye of wisdom. The same eyes now see something deeper, because thinking has moved beyond fixed categories such as yes/no and good/bad.
Opening poem: to be for or against any ideology, your stomach must first be full. Philosophy needs a full stomach and free time, which humans did not have for most of their history.
The most popular branch: what is the world ultimately, what is it made of, and where does its diversity come from. Its three deepest questions concern creation, God and the soul.

Creationism says God made it; evolutionism says it developed on its own; a middle view says God set a basic structure and evolution did the rest. The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, the Earth about 4.5 billion and life about 3.7 billion. The speaker corrected his earlier slip, when he had given the universe's age as the Earth's.
Some traditions believe in God; Jainism and Buddhism do not; Taoism and Confucianism hold God differently. Believers then ask what God is like and what He does.

About 70,000 to 75,000 years ago, Homo sapiens' larger brain, its prefrontal cortex and language allowed complex thought, shared rules, morals and the state. Brain size alone is not the answer: an elephant's brain is larger.
About 10,000 years ago humans learned farming, no longer had to wander or kill for every meal, and gained surplus and leisure. Systematic thinking, philosophy and science grew from this.
Regarded as the West's first philosopher, in the 6th century BC, only about 2,800 years ago. The speaker warns against claims that philosophy is millions of years old.
Parmenides, Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Aristotle and Herodotus belong to the same era, when a few Greek cities had the leisure and conditions to think.

Niyativada versus Sankalpa Swatantrya: do we really choose our actions? Determinism is the stronger argument, yet society cannot punish, reward or function without assuming free will, so we proceed as if it is real.

German pessimist, nicknamed the 'Frankfurt Buddha' because he read Buddhism and the Upanishads all his life. He often used Sophocles' line that the best is never to be born, and called himself a pessimist, which helped spread the label to the Buddha. The speaker says Indian thought differs: it names suffering but ends in liberation.
The study of how we know. If you claim something is true, philosophy asks for your Pramana: perception, inference, or testimony.
The Vedas and Upanishads. Most ideas Hindus hold today (soul, Moksha, rebirth) were already settled by the Upanishads.
A reaction to heavy ritual and animal sacrifice. Charvaka, Jainism and Buddhism arise.
The Vedas are reinstated as proof. Short memory-friendly sutras give us the six Astika schools.
Around the time Islam arrived, scholars wrote Bhashyas on the Vedanta sutras. Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva, the Bhakti saints and Sikhism belong here.
19th and 20th century India's own renaissance and reform, giving Neo-Vedanta. The speaker compares it with Europe's Renaissance and Reformation.
The speaker adds a sixth phase: Ambedkar, Krishnamurti and Osho, with Iqbal just before independence.
After the Vedas and Upanishads, books recognise nine schools: three Nastika (Charvaka, Jain, Buddhist) and six Astika.
In this classification it is not about God or the afterlife. Astika means accepting the Vedas as proof; Nastika means not taking them as proof just because they are written.

Charvaka, Lokayata and the Brihaspati tradition are treated as one school: a group rather than one person, called Dehatmavada (the living body is the soul). It accepts perception alone as proof, so it drops inference, testimony and the unseen: no God, no soul, no rebirth, no karma, no heaven, hell or Moksha. The world is four elements (not five, since space cannot be perceived) that meet by their own nature in different proportions; consciousness arises from them as the red of chewed betel arises from ingredients none of which is red. Its goal is pleasure in this life: 'live happily as long as you live; borrow and drink ghee'. The speaker's 'drink, fall, rise, drink again' verse is traced by scholars to the Kularnava Tantra, not to Charvaka. Its own books are lost; we know it through critics, chiefly the Sarvadarshanasangraha. The speaker's view: its ethics are one-sided, but it kept Indian thought from hardening into dogma, and its materialism deserves a fair hearing today.

Charvaka is believed to have grown from the teaching of Brihaspati, a name that also belongs to the gods' teacher in myth. The speaker says there were many Brihaspatis and that some identify this one with Vatsyayana, author of the Kamasutra; that is his guess, and the Kamasutra's author is dated to about the 3rd century CE. Texts attribute a lost Brihaspati Sutra to this line, known only through quotations.

A materialist teacher of the Charvaka or Lokayata line, a contemporary of the Buddha, named for his hair blanket (kesa-kambala). The lecture calls him the first Indian voice to say plainly that there is no soul, heaven, hell, rebirth or karma, and compares him with Leucippus and Democritus. The Pali texts give him four elements that return to their sources at death; gifts and sacrifices bear no fruit. The speaker offers a reason for the blanket (training to bear heat and cold) and doubts it; Buddhist texts instead call it the poorest of garments. 'Ajita' means 'unconquered', because he was said to be hard to beat in debate.

The view that the body is the soul: consciousness belongs to a living body, and when the body dies it is gone. The speaker points out that the school mixes up 'soul' and 'consciousness', since other schools hold that consciousness is only a feature of the soul. It is the Indian ancestor of the modern view that mind is something brains do.

The modern echo of Charvaka's claim: mind emerges from physical neurons working together, as intoxication emerges from fermented grain. The speaker says science is moving toward this view; critics reply that how matter produces felt experience is still unexplained (the hard problem).
Does not believe in God. Mahavira is the 24th Tirthankara.

The 24th Tirthankara, living in roughly the same region and era as the Buddha (present-day Bihar). By the speaker's arithmetic he died at Pava about a year after the Buddha's enlightenment; the Buddha's own last meal was in the same town 44 years later. Makkhali Gosala walked with him for six years before parting. There is no record that the two met.
A profound Jain view of knowledge and the limits of statements. The speaker says it is a deep basis of what we now call Artificial Intelligence.
Rejects the Vedas as proof and a permanent soul, but accepts rebirth and Moksha.

Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda. Mostly mantras for ritual and worship; little philosophy in the early parts. Some give them 10,000 years; the generally accepted view dates their composition to about 1500 BCE, give or take two or three centuries.
Samhita (mantras), Brahmana (procedures), Aranyaka (conduct of forest dwellers) and Upanishad.
The last part of the Vedas, hence 'Vedanta': pure philosophy. Soul, Moksha and rebirth are fixed here.
Mimamsa's claim: the Vedas were not composed even by God; they are eternal and uncreated.
Those who accept the Vedas as Pramana. Six of them make the Shad Darshan, called Hindu or Sanatana philosophy.
The six: Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa and Vedanta, working in joint pairs.
Formulas that state a profound idea very briefly so it can be remembered before writing was common. They are hard to understand without commentary.
Paired with Yoga. Its sutra is attributed to Sage Kapila, though the original text has not been found.
Close companion of Samkhya in one group.
Paired with Vaisheshika; its Sutra is by Akshapada Gautama.
Works jointly with Nyaya, each accepting what the other develops.
Treats the Vedas as uncreated; its idea of Moksha is lighter than Vedanta's.
The dominant school. The speaker says 90 to 95 per cent of what Hindus believe is Vedanta. Its sources are the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutra.
Author of the Samkhya Sutra.
Wrote the Nyaya Sutra (not the same Gautama as the Buddha).
Author of the Brahma Sutra; some identify him with Ved Vyasa.

Teaches Vedanta and is the text most Hindus identify with. It states the immortal soul most clearly. The ethics lecture draws four principles from it (Nishkama Karma Yoga, Sthitaprajna, Lokasangraha, avatarism) and adds Swadharma; the transcript covers only the first and Swadharma. Historians place the Gita inside the Mahabharata (Bhishma Parva) and date it roughly between the 2nd century BCE and the 2nd century CE (added for context).
Because sutras are cryptic, scholars explained them. Interpreting Vedanta meant commenting on the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutra.
From South India, died at 32 after building a profound philosophy. Said only Brahman is ultimately real.
Only Brahman is the absolute truth. God, we and the world are true only at the practical level, like a video game you can step out of.
The world and even God are true on the vyavaharika (practical) level; only Brahman is true in the end.

Mahayana philosopher of South India (Nagarjunakonda in Andhra), about 150 CE, who explained Avyakrita through Madhyamaka Shunyavada and made the four-cornered logic famous. His ideas resemble Shankara's so closely that some call Shankara a 'disguised Buddhist'. He is not Nagasena, the monk who debated King Milinda.
Devotees of Vishnu who challenged Shankara by putting devotion at the centre.
The first to take Shankara head-on, with Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism).
Active around Agra, Mathura and Vrindavan; Ballabhgarh is named after him. Surdas was his devotee.
Gave Dvaitadvaita.
From Karnataka and Shankara's fiercest critic; his philosophy is Dvaita (dualism).
Great devotee of Krishna; his school is Achintya Bhedabheda (inconceivable difference and non-difference).
The shared purpose of the Vaishnava Acharyas: to establish the tradition of devotion.
In Ramanuja's line; his student was Kabir Das.
Bhakti saint; many of his verses are in the Guru Granth Sahib.
Bhakti poet in Ramanuja's tradition.
Founder of Sikhism, close to Kabir in outlook; the Guru Granth Sahib holds many verses of Kabir. He saw God as formless and without attributes (nirguna) and taught Ek Onkar, one supreme power.

A philosophical development of the 15th–16th century, rising when Kabir was active; it holds karma and rebirth. The speaker argues it belongs in histories of Indian philosophy, since a philosophy born in India is Indian; most textbooks stop at Madhva.
Vedanta reshaped in the 19th century to present Hinduism as one, answer Western charges of division, and tie philosophy to nationalism and equality.
The scholar who coined 'Neo-Vedanta', sarcastically, since it made converting Hindus harder.
Started the Brahmo Samaj, combining Hindu beliefs with Unitarian Christian ideas, and addressed malpractices.
Priest at a Kali temple who became Narendranath's teacher.
Narendranath Datta, the most prominent symbol of Neo-Vedanta.
Freedom fighter turned philosopher: Integral Yoga.
Took both Neo-Vedanta and Vaishnava Vedanta along.
His philosophy is in the same Neo-Vedanta stream.

Composed the Satyarth Prakash and founded the Arya Samaj. He called for a return to the Vedas, yet many of his beliefs stand close to Neo-Vedanta. His movement stresses logic, rejects caste, backs gender equality and girls' education, and keeps its distance from Christianity and Islam. The DAV schools (Dayanand Anglo-Vedic) joined Vedic learning with English education.
Neo-Vedanta's main work: treating the world as real and worth acting in, against the view that the world is mithya and freedom an illusion.
Poet-philosopher just before independence. His philosophy is universalistic and falls outside Neo-Vedanta and Hinduism, yet the speaker counts it as important.

Found that caste endured, converted to Buddhism in 1956, and wrote The Buddha and His Dhamma. He rejected traditional karma and Nirvana to create Navayana. The Gita lecture names him as the Gita's leading critic on Varna: he read the text as a defence of the caste order.
Ambedkar's new form of Buddhist philosophy, begun in 1956 in the 20th century.

Brought up under Annie Besant of the Theosophical Society, who became his guardian after a long custody dispute with his father (the speaker says 'adopted'). He later rejected all organised religion and gave a philosophy that is popular especially in South India.

Taught philosophy at a college in Jabalpur, left it, and became a teacher of meditation. He built Rajneeshpuram in the US, came back to India and settled in Pune, where he died in 1990. The speaker admires his habit of answering every question and says he freed religion of stereotypes. His 'dynamic meditation' means meditation can be done while dancing; he wrote a book on Lao Tzu. The speaker's advice to students: link dance and philosophy by becoming Osho.

The speaker names Lopamudra, Maitreyi, Gargi and Ghosha, then says participation almost vanishes until Mirabai and a few modern women. He blames the glass ceiling and the limits of household life, not the capacity of women. He adds that the first women philosophers in the world are found in India, since Indian thought is older than Greek. Scholars place Lopamudra and Ghosha in the Rigveda rather than the Upanishads; Maitreyi and Gargi are in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

Born a Shakya prince at Kapilavastu. Tradition dates him about 563–483 BCE, though many scholars place him later. He left home at about 29, awoke at 35, taught for some 45 years and died at 80. The speaker says he was less a philosopher than a reformer who wanted society to stop suffering.

Two accounts. In the Buddhacharita, the four sights led him to leave one night on his horse Kanthaka with the charioteer Channa, who turned back at the Anoma river. In Ambedkar's account he left in place of a war: the whole community walked with him to the river and he asked them to go home and stop the fighting.

nodes.l: Sujata's kheer and the Middle Path
nodes.d: After six years of severe penance a woman named Sujata offered him a bowl of rice milk. He ate, bathed in the river and saw that the body must stay healthy to seek truth. His five companions, thinking he had fallen away, left him. The meal marked the turn to the Middle Path.
Questions the Buddha would not answer, because they do not help end suffering. Not ignorance but a crisis of expression.
Four-cornered logic: is it, is it not, both, neither. Each question about the world, soul or Tathagata was answered by none of the four.
Treat the wounded first, not the theory. Human civilisation is wounded; the task is relief.
Equal arguments for and against mean a question cannot be proven; mystical experience cannot be put into ordinary language.

18th-century German philosopher the speaker cites for a similar view that some questions cannot be settled by reason: he found equally strong arguments for and against, which he called antinomies. On the self he allowed a logical (unifying) self but no experienced soul, so he stayed agnostic in theory, and held God and the soul as practical needs for morality. The speaker names the 'Critique of Pure Reason' for this last step; it belongs to the Critique of Practical Reason.

Sarvam Dukkham (suffering), its cause in ignorance and craving, its cessation (Nirvana) and the path to it. Framed like a doctor's diagnosis. 'Arya' here means noble or wise, one who has understood the truths, not a race.

Even what we call happiness is suffering: it costs effort to get, anxiety to keep and pain to lose, and it is relative, so someone else's gain turns it sour (the speaker's examples: exam years, the gym, a retired official's first day). Only the Charvakas and, the speaker says, Vaishnava Vedanta resist the claim; most Indian schools agree the world is full of suffering.

The eight limbs of the path to end suffering: right view, resolve, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration. The canon groups them as wisdom (the first two), conduct (the next three) and meditation (the last three). The lecture's grouping differs slightly and its transcript garbles several names, so the graph follows the canon. The Jain 'three jewels' are a comparable triad.
The end of suffering (Dukkha Nirodha).

No permanent soul exists; a person is a stream of consciousness joined to a body, and the stream carries the impressions of karma. The speaker explains rebirth by one flame lighting another: the flame is similar, yet not identical.

One of the early schools after the Buddha, keeper of the Pali canon, which was first written down in Sri Lanka. Theravada is the Pali form of Sthaviravada, 'the way of the elders'. 'Hinayana' (small vehicle) is a Mahayana insult, not the school's own name. The speaker thinks it stays closest to the Buddha; scholars say all later schools shaped the record.
Grew from the Mahasanghika line; it considers Moksha as supreme bliss and accepts transfer of merit (Parinamana).
Later school within Mahayana, alongside Tantrayana and Mantrayana.
His last words: be your own light.

Whatever you do will return to you: today's life repays the past and tomorrow repays today. Two rules: what you did cannot perish before it bears fruit (kritanasha), and what you did not do cannot reach you (akritabhyagama). So karma cannot be transferred. The speaker notes that Hinduism has no 'debit and credit' of merit between people. The Mahayana idea of the Bodhisattva does let merit be shared, and Christianity's atonement lets one person bear another's sins. Every Indian school except Charvaka accepts karma, including Sikhism.

Sanchita (accumulated, to bear fruit later), Prarabdha (now bearing fruit; what we call fate or 'prarabdha') and Kriyamana (being done now, its fruit still to come). The speaker's picture: the course of the next five years is shaped by the stored Sanchita; today's actions are the future's Sanchita.

A conscious, immortal, eternal element in the body. Needed so that the person who acts is the person who reaps: someone who dies before his karma ripens must still face it. Seven of nine schools hold it; only Charvaka and Buddhism deny it. The Gita states it most clearly: weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it, wind cannot dry it. Schools differ on what the soul is; see 'Indian views of the soul compared'.
Almost every Indian school except Charvaka holds it. It explains birth into poverty or wealth, and even justified caste, which some criticise.

Almost all Indian schools agree. Samkhya counts three kinds: Adhyatmika (from one's own body and mind), Adhibhautika (from other beings) and Adhidaivika (from supernatural forces such as floods and quakes). In this lecture the speaker names Charvaka and Vaishnava Vedanta as the exceptions: Vaishnavas say a soul that is part of God cannot be sad, and sorrow comes only from wrong action. Indian thought begins with suffering but ends in liberation.

Liberation from the cycle of karma and rebirth. The balance of karma at death decides the next birth, which may even be non-human; when the balance reaches zero there is no rebirth. It is permanent, with no probation. Names differ: Nirvana (Buddhist), Kaivalya (Jain), Apavarga (Nyaya), Nihshreyas (Mimamsa), liberation (Shankara). Meanings differ too: see 'Negative and positive Moksha'. The Semitic goal is heaven. Eight of nine schools hold Moksha as life's purpose; Charvaka does not.
The root of bondage: we take ourselves to be the body.
Liberation comes through knowledge, though some add devotion or action.
The valid source of knowledge: every claim must name its evidence. Schools disagree on how many sources count, from one (Charvaka) to six (Advaita Vedanta and Bhatta Mimamsa).

Pythagoras, Plato and Socrates spoke of it; Giordano Bruno defended it; Ian Stevenson studied claims of past lives for 40 years. Judaism, Christianity and Islam mostly reject it, though some Sufis and the Jewish idea of Gilgul touch it. The speaker says science has not proved rebirth; he calls the matter debated and open.
The branch about values. It has two parts: ethics and aesthetics.
What is moral and what is not; whether moral rules should bend over time (is lying to save someone a sin?); what the purpose of life is; and what is good in itself, not merely as a means.

The study of beauty. Is beauty in the eye of the beholder (subjectivism), in the thing itself (objectivism), or shaped by culture? The speaker adds that even the beholder's eye is largely made by culture.
The third question of metaphysics: what are mind, intelligence and consciousness, and is there a soul beyond the body? Psychology began as part of philosophy.

The old claim that the world is made of atoms, made in India by Nyaya and Vaisheshika, and by Makkhali Gosala, the Jains and some Buddhist schools (the speaker adds more), and in Greece by Leucippus and Democritus in the 5th century BCE, about 2,300 years before science (Dalton, 1803). Philosophy reached it by thought, not experiment, and the atom of science differs from theirs.

17th-century philosopher: 'I think, therefore I am'. The body does not think, so something else does, and that is the soul. The lecture sets the cogito beside the empiricists, but Descartes was a rationalist who trusted reason over the senses, the opposite of the Charvaka method.
Computers reason, remember and now write stories without any soul, which puts pressure on the idea that thinking needs a soul and gives the Charvaka view a new hearing.
Kant's view: we cannot know about God or the soul. So believe if you wish, and do not trouble others for believing or not.
Seeing is not proof: the light, the senses or the mind's categories may each distort what we perceive (a fat dog taken for a small cow). Strong emotion or chemicals cause hallucinations.
Science assumes every event has a cause. Nyaya and Buddhist thinkers examined this; Hume called it an inductive habit, like concluding all pigeons are black after seeing a hundred.

18th-century British philosopher who questioned cause and effect as only a habit of mind. Looking inward for a self, he found only passing sensations and so could not claim a soul exists; the speaker sets this beside the Buddha's stream of consciousness, which came about 2,000 years earlier.

Philosophy and science grew fastest where meditation, open discussion and freedom to think existed, even if not for everyone. The speaker places Indian philosophy at about 4,000 years and the Greek tradition from about 600 BC.
The speaker's own conclusion after studying philosophy: you learn that nobody knows the answers, and that you know as much as anyone does. A book distils decades of someone's thought into a few days.
Philosophy is applied to every field: of history, science, religion, politics. Each asks the deepest questions about how that field works.
Upanishadic statements such as Aham Brahmasmi, Tat tvam asi and Ayam Atma Brahma: the self (Atman) is Brahman.
Knowing one's original nature. In Indian philosophy it is knowledge of the soul or of what I am and am not. Mahavira, the Buddha, Shankara and Nanak are cited as examples.

nodes.l: Mysticism and the limit of language
nodes.d: Ordinary words come from ordinary shared experience, so a mystical experience has none. 'Mysticism' comes from muo, to be silent. Kabir's dumb man tasting jaggery and Rahim's verse make the same point.

In a dream we do not know it is a dream until we wake. Nagarjuna, the Buddhist brothers Asanga and Vasubandhu, and Shankara asked whether this practical world is a dream too. The speaker says it is a logical possibility, unproven, so we live as if life is real.
Buddhist philosopher brothers, grouped with Nagarjuna and Shankara for their similar views on the dream-like practical world.

For the common person, easy answers to hard questions and an organisation of beliefs. It offers peace, such as the soul being immortal so death only changes clothes. In India religion and philosophy work together toward ending suffering; in the West, especially in Greece, they are far apart.

From adhi + atma: connecting with something greater than oneself, whether God, Nirvana, Kaivalya, knowledge, or a feeling of unity with the whole world (extrovert mysticism). One can be spiritual without religion.

In the 6th century BCE iron tools spread across the Ganga plain. More land was ploughed and yields rose, giving farmers a surplus. Towns, markets and coined money followed. The speaker's rule: a philosopher says what his circumstances call for, so the Buddha cannot be understood without this world.

Small tribal territories merged into larger states, mostly monarchies and a few republics (gana-sanghas). Magadha (Rajgir), Kosala (Shravasti), the Vajji-Licchavi republic (Vaishali) and the Mallas (Kushinagar) frame the Buddha's whole life. Taxes paid for armies and wars; Kapilavastu of the Shakyas survived as a protected state of Kosala.

Kshatriyas and Vaishyas gained power and wealth but little standing in the Brahmin-led ritual order. Both Jainism and Buddhism came from Kshatriya founders and drew strong merchant support. The speaker reads this as a search for religious respect to match economic weight; it is one historians' interpretation, not proof of motive.

Around the 6th century BCE new ways of thinking appeared independently in several lands: the Shramanas in India, Confucius and Lao Tzu in China, Pythagoras and Heraclitus in Greece, Zoroaster in Persia. The term is Karl Jaspers'. The speaker also lists Thales, Shinto and Moses. Historians qualify two of these: Moses, if historical, belongs to about the 13th century BCE (the Torah took its present form later), and Shinto has no founding date.
Greek thinker (about 500 BCE) who held that everything flows and no one steps into the same river twice. The speaker sets his impermanence beside the Buddha's; no link between them is known.
Greek mathematician and philosopher who also taught rebirth, which shows the idea was not only Indian.

Wandering ascetic teachers who challenged the Vedic ritual order and caste hierarchy. Buddhist texts speak of sixty-two views; seven teachers were famous and the Buddha was one. Six ran alongside him: Mahavira, Makkhali Gosala, Ajita Kesakambali, Purana Kassapa, Pakudha Kaccayana and Sanjaya Belatthiputta.

Compassion was one reason for the new stress on non-violence. Another was economic: ploughing needed cattle, and costly animal sacrifices drained farmers. Jains avoided farming because it harms living things in the soil and moved into trade, which helps explain their later prosperity.

Walked with Mahavira for about six years, then split from him. He founded the Ajivikas and taught that everything is fixed in advance. The speaker notes that his determinism is about 2,000 years older than Spinoza's, and that he spoke of atoms before the Greeks (the Ajivikas did hold an atomic theory).
Fatalist ascetic sect that rose with Makkhali Gosala. It held that outcomes are fixed whatever one does. It later faded from history.

Everything is destined, so deeds do not change the outcome. The speaker says people drift to it after disappointment, such as failing an exam after hard work. It conflicts with karma: if results follow actions, they cannot also be fated.

Taught agnosticism and scepticism: he would not say yes or no on rebirth, karma or the afterlife, since no one really knows. Sariputta and Moggallana were his best pupils before they went over to the Buddha. The speaker pairs him with Kant and Pyrrho in the West.

Taught that actions carry no moral consequence: nothing is sin or merit, whether one kills or gives alms on the banks of the Ganga (the example in the Pali sutta). He is reported to have claimed to know everything and, in the tradition, to have drowned himself. The speaker calls this amoralism and says no act can be called moral in an absolute sense. The Buddha strongly opposed him, since denying karma risked spreading immorality.

Taught seven eternal elements: earth, water, fire, air, pleasure, pain and life. Since they only combine and separate, a sword passing through a body kills no one. The lecture runs him together with Ajita; the early texts list them as separate teachers.

The Jain view that reality has many sides, so every claim is partial. The speaker links it to the habit of saying 'I may be wrong' and to the Jain festival of forgiveness, when people ask pardon for the year's wrongs.

Part 1 is the Buddha's life. Part 2 is his own philosophy; Part 3 the Hinayana schools; Part 4 the Mahayana, with Shunyavada, Vijnanavada and Vajrayana; Part 5 the Navayana. After Buddhism the speaker plans the Vedic texts and the Gita, Shankara and Vaishnava Vedanta, the other Darshans, Western philosophy, philosophy of religion, and questions of equality and justice.

Vinaya Pitaka (monastic rules), Sutta Pitaka (the discourses) and Abhidhamma Pitaka (the deep philosophy, traditionally finished under Ashoka around 250 BCE). The Sutta Pitaka has five collections, including the Digha Nikaya, with the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, and the Khuddaka Nikaya, with the Jatakas, Dhammapada and Therigatha.

Called by King Ajatashatru of Magadha right after the Buddha's death, because his words might otherwise scatter. Upali, a barber by birth, recited the Vinaya; Ananda recited the discourses. Nothing was written; everything was memorised and chanted.
The texts stayed oral until they were written on palm leaves in Sri Lanka about 29 BCE, some 450 years after the Buddha's death. The long oral gap is one reason the life story has layers.

About 547 stories of the Buddha's earlier births, collected in the Khuddaka Nikaya. They are moral folklore: good evidence for what people believed, weak evidence for his life. The Kunala Jataka mentions the Rohini river quarrel.

Verses by about seventy-three early Buddhist nuns telling how they left home and walked the path. The speaker counts it among the most moving books in world literature and as proof that women had a real voice in the early community.

Poet-philosopher of the 1st–2nd century CE, linked to the Kushan king Kanishka and to the Mahayana. His Buddhacharita is the great Sanskrit life of the Buddha, which the speaker ranks with Kalidasa's work.

Ashvaghosha's Sanskrit poem in 28 cantos, of which only the first half survives in Sanskrit; the rest returns through Tibetan and Chinese translations. It gave the popular story of the four sights, with gods steering events, and reads the life through Mahayana eyes about five centuries after the Buddha.
A Mahayana sutra that tells the life with the most miracles: the Buddha descends from Tushita heaven, is born painlessly and takes seven steps. Historians read it as devotion built up over centuries.

Early Pali texts are sparse; Ashvaghosha dramatises the life; the Lalitavistara adds miracles; Ambedkar rewrites it on rational lines. The speaker's method is to tell both the traditional story and the Navayana one, and to say plainly which parts rest on thin evidence.

Ambedkar's book, finished in 1956 and published in 1957 after his death, meant as a Buddhist guide for India. It strips out the supernatural, rewrites the life, and drops traditional karma and rebirth. Traditional Buddhists objected that it should be called Ambedkar's Dhamma.

He doubted that a man of 28–29 had never seen age, illness or death; that a scientific mind would call all existence suffering; that a teacher of no-soul would also hold rebirth and Nirvana; and that a monks' order outside productive social life could be useful. His new account rests on these doubts.

In Ambedkar's account the Shakyas and Koliyas quarrelled over the Rohini river. The Shakya council voted for war and conscription; Siddhartha opposed it and faced exile, execution or his family's disgrace, and chose to leave as a monk so the war could be averted. The speaker finds the evidence thin: it rests on a Marathi biography, a Jataka and Kosambi, and the Jataka puts the dispute after his renunciation.
Maharashtrian social reformer and teacher who gave the young Ambedkar, after his school success, his Marathi life of the Buddha (published 1898). It already carried the Rohini story.

Scholar of Pali Buddhism whose Marathi Bhagavan Buddha (1940) and play Bodhisattva (1949) carry the Rohini theme. He was the father of the Marxist historian D. D. Kosambi, whom the lecture's wording blurs with him.

Queen Maya, travelling to her parents' home, gave birth in the Lumbini grove, now in Nepal. His mother died a week later and her sister Mahapajapati raised him. His father was Suddhodana of the Shakya clan at Kapilavastu. Miracles such as the seven steps come from later books.

Court dream-readers and the sage Asita foretold that the child would be a universal emperor or a great renouncer who becomes a Buddha. Asita wept because he would not live to see it. Suddhodana, fearing the second outcome, tried to make renunciation impossible.

He studied the Vedas and grammar, learned meditation and trained as a warrior, excelling at all. Gentle by nature, he shunned the hunt. When a bird he sheltered was claimed by his cousin Devadatta, who had shot it, the council ruled for the one who saved it, and the rivalry began.

His father arranged a marriage with Yashodhara, who chose him in a contest of skills over rival suitors. Accounts differ on ages; the lecture gives 20 and 16. Their son Rahula came years later. Suddhodana added seasonal palaces and a court of dancers to bind him to home.

In the Buddhacharita, outings showed him an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering mendicant, each arranged by the gods. He decided that day to renounce. Ambedkar doubted that a man of 29 had never seen old age, sickness or death.

After leaving, he went to Rajgir. Alara Kalama and then Uddaka Ramaputta taught him successively higher meditative states. He mastered them in days but saw the peace was personal and temporary, so the world's suffering was untouched. The lecture links them with Samkhya-Yoga and its three kinds of suffering; the early texts describe only the meditation levels.

King of Magadha at Rajgir. He offered the young seeker half his kingdom or a life of ease; the Buddha refused but promised to return. He later became a lay follower and gave the Veluvana garden to the monks. His son Ajatashatru starved him to death.

At Uruvela, by the Niranjana river, with five companions (Kondanna, Vappa, Bhaddiya, Mahanama and Assaji), he ate a bowl of rice and then a grain a day, wore rags and slept in cemeteries. After six years he saw that a starving body could not know anything and gave the path up.

After Sujata's meal he sat facing east under the pipal tree at Gaya, vowing not to rise without knowledge. At 35 he found answers to his two questions: why is there suffering, and how does it end. The lecture speaks of weeks of sitting; the early texts speak of one night's awakening.

He hesitated for seven weeks over whether to teach. People rely on God, a soul and heaven, and his truth offered none, so he feared no one would grasp it. A god (Brahma) is said to have asked him to teach for the world's sake, and he agreed.

He walked to Sarnath and found his five former companions. Their anger melted as he came near; they washed his feet and heard the Four Noble Truths. They took refuge, saying this was a teaching with no prophet, no single scripture and no miracle. This turning of the wheel of Dhamma began the community.

Yasa, a rich Varanasi youth sickened by a life of luxury, was won over within minutes. His parents and wife became the first lay followers and four friends became monks. With sixty monks trained, the Buddha sent them out to teach for the good of many.

Three matted-haired fire-worshipping brothers, Uruvela, Nadi and Gaya Kassapa, led about a thousand disciples. The Buddha won the proudest, Uruvela, by patient argument (the texts add legends of a fire-breathing serpent). They threw their sacrificial vessels into the river and joined him. At Rajgir, Bimbisara and a vast crowd followed.

Childhood friends and pupils of Sanjaya, seeking a better teacher. Assaji, one of the five, explained the Dhamma to Sariputta, and both joined the Buddha with 250 followers. Sariputta, the 'commander of the Dhamma', was famed for reasoning. They died before the Buddha, Sariputta in his native village and Moggallana at the hands of enemies.

Sudatta, a Shravasti banker known for feeding orphans. After a short talk he asked whether he must leave his wealth and work to become a monk; the Buddha said no. He bought Prince Jeta's garden by covering it with gold coins and built the Jetavana monastery.

The garden at Shravasti given by Prince Jeta and Anathapindika. The Buddha is said to have spent about nineteen rainy seasons there; the rains retreat is when monks stay in one place for four months. King Prasenajit of Kosala became a devotee but did not take robes.
King of Kosala at Shravasti and overlord of the Shakyas. He respected the Buddha, talked with him at length, and asked his help over the robber Angulimala. His son Jeta gave the Jetavana garden.

Head of the Shakya clan at Kapilavastu and the Buddha's father. The lecture shows him as a clan leader bound by the council rather than an absolute king. He feared the prophecy of renunciation, worked to keep his son at home, and died after the Buddha's return.

Wife of Siddhartha and mother of Rahula. Her anger at his leaving unannounced, and her later dignity, are retold by Maithili Sharan Gupta and, in a new way, by Ambedkar, who has her approve his going. She became the nun Bhadda Kaccana and, in his account, died the year he did.

Maya's sister (the lecture calls her the elder; the texts usually say younger), Suddhodana's second wife and the Buddha's foster mother. She led five hundred women to demand ordination and became the first nun.
The Buddha's only son, born about eight years after the marriage. On the Kapilavastu visit he asked his father for his inheritance and received the Dhamma, entering the community as a boy.

Cousin, son of Amitodana, and the Buddha's long-time attendant. He pleaded for the nuns, stood by the Buddha at his death and recited the discourses at the First Council. The lecture calls him the person closest to the Buddha.

Messengers sent by Suddhodana joined the Buddha and forgot to return, until Kaludayi persuaded him. The Buddha stayed in the Nigrodha garden and begged in his father's city; his father protested, and he answered that begging was the custom of his own lineage, the line of Buddhas. Yashodhara waited in her room; he went to her and she wept at his feet. Young Rahula asked for his inheritance and was given the Dhamma.

Court barber who shaved the heads of the Shakya princes (Ananda, Anuruddha, Bhaddiya and others) when they renounced. They asked the Buddha to ordain him first so that he would outrank them. He became the master of the Vinaya and recited it at the First Council.

After Suddhodana died, Mahapajapati Gotami and some five hundred Shakya women shaved their heads and walked to Vaishali. The Buddha refused three times, fearing practical dangers: angry families, quarrels, attacks. Ananda argued that women could reach liberation and that history would judge him, and the Buddha agreed on conditions. Yashodhara joined as Bhadda Kaccana; Amrapali joined later.

A feared robber in Kosala who killed travellers and wore their fingers as a garland, aiming for a thousand. The Buddha walked on calmly; when told to stop, he answered that he had stopped and the robber had not. Angulimala gave up violence and became a monk. He was stoned when he begged, and the Buddha told him to bear it.

Cousin and rival from the wounded-bird story. After joining the community he gained little power. When the Buddha was about 72 he asked to lead the Sangha and was refused. He then plotted with Prince Ajatashatru to kill Bimbisara and the Buddha.

Prince who killed his father Bimbisara and became king of Magadha, conquered the Vajji republic and sought the courtesan Amrapali. Haunted by guilt, he met the Buddha with Jivaka's help. He called the First Council after the Buddha's death.
Famed physician of Bimbisara, Ajatashatru and the Buddha. Texts credit him with remarkable surgeries, though how far they are authentic is uncertain.

Ajatashatru starved his father Bimbisara and took the throne. Devadatta's trained assassins could not strike the Buddha; a rolled boulder hurt his foot; the elephant sent to trample him did not attack. Ajatashatru later felt remorse, and Jivaka brought him to the Buddha, who forgave him.

City courtesan (nagarvadhu) of Vaishali, a respected role that forbade marriage. She invited the Buddha to a meal before the Licchavi princes could and would not give way to them. She gave her mango grove to the Sangha and became a nun. Another story says Ajatashatru loved her and used the tie to take Vaishali.

Sariputta and Moggallana died, Moggallana killed by enemies. In Ambedkar's account Mahapajapati and Yashodhara, both about 78–80, came to say farewell and died soon after; other traditions say Yashodhara outlived him. She spoke only gratitude for having known such a husband.

On his last journey he looked back at Vaishali, then ate at the house of Chunda the smith in Pava a dish called sukara-maddava, which some read as pork and others as a mushroom. Ill but calm, he bathed in the Kukuttha river, walked on to Kushinagar and died there after teaching his last disciple, Subhadda. He told Ananda that Chunda was blameless.

nodes.l: Funeral and the eight relic shares
nodes.d: The Mallas gave the body a royal cremation after a week of preparation. Ajatashatru, the Licchavis, the Shakyas and others armed themselves to claim the relics. The Brahmin Drona asked how followers of a man of peace could fight over his ashes, and divided them into eight equal shares for stupas, keeping the urn.

When A is present, B arises. Everything arises from conditions, so nothing in the world is its own cause. This rejects both chance (as in Charvaka) and a supernatural cause beyond the world, and the speaker says the one sentence ends God as first cause in Buddhist thought. It also gives the Second Truth its cause: the twelve links from ignorance to old age and death.

nodes.l: Dhamma without prophet, book or miracle
nodes.d: What struck the five companions was a teaching with no god-given authority, no single scripture and no miracle: events follow natural causes. The speaker stresses that the Buddha refused to be a prophet, so followers must test the Dhamma by their own conscience.

In life, the path between palace luxury and six years of near-starvation, tied to Sujata's bowl. In doctrine, the path between eternalism (something lasts for ever, such as a soul or God) and annihilationism (everything simply ends at death): nothing is eternal and nothing ends, because each state gives rise to the next. The lecture also reads it as moderation in pleasure and pain, and links it to right livelihood.

The Buddha told Anathapindika that riches are not evil; the harm comes when money rules the mind. Someone who earns well and uses wealth for society serves it better than a monk. The speaker compares this with Gandhi's trusteeship and links it to Right Livelihood in the Eightfold Path.

Sotapanna (stream-enterer, at most seven more births), Sakadagami (one more), Anagami (none) and Arhat, who is liberated while alive and does not return. The Jains use Arihant for a similar ideal. Anathapindika became a stream-enterer after a short talk.

nodes.l: The Sangha and the rains retreat
nodes.d: The community of monks and nuns, supported by lay followers who gave food and land. Its rules are in the Vinaya. Monks begged each morning and meditated; for four months of the rains they stayed in one place, which is how monasteries grew. Ambedkar asked what such a body did for society.

The community took in people of any birth: Upali the barber, Sunita the scavenger, Sopaka and Suppiya who worked at the cremation ground, and the nun Prakriti of Chandala birth. Ananda used this record when he pleaded for women's entry.

Conditions for the nuns, such as that a nun, however senior, ranks below any monk and may not rebuke one. The speaker sees them partly as a practical bargain in a world hostile to women's orders; critics call them bias. He also notes the remark, probably later, that women's entry would halve the Dhamma's life.

Ananda asked who would lead. The Buddha named no one: the Dhamma would guide and the Sangha would decide together. The Pali texts say Mahavira's community quarrelled after his death. The Buddha left no ruler, no prophet's role and no sacred book; his last advice was to be a lamp unto oneself.

nodes.l: 'If you meet the Buddha, kill him'
nodes.d: A Zen saying (the transcript says Jainism, which looks like a mis-hearing) that the seeker should not lean on statues, books or even the teacher. The speaker's story of the monk who would call a plumber for a flushed scripture and sweep up a broken statue makes the same point: the Dhamma matters, not its objects.

In the Mahayana, a being bound for Buddhahood over many lives, passing ten stages. Stories of the Buddha's descent from Tushita heaven belong to this later view; the early texts do not have them. The speaker traces the Mahayana to the Mahasanghika split about a century after the Buddha; the full Mahayana took shape later.

Early school whose name means 'everything exists'. The speaker announces it for Part 3 with two branches, which I read as Vaibhashika and Sautrantika because the transcript garbles the names. Not yet taught in this lecture.
Mahayana school of emptiness, founded by Nagarjuna. Announced for Part 4; not yet taught in this lecture.
Mahayana school of consciousness, tied to Asanga and Vasubandhu. Announced for Part 4; not yet taught in this lecture.

The tradition names Vyasa as compiler of the Vedas, author of the 18 Puranas and the Mahabharata (with the Gita), and some say of the Brahma Sutra. The speaker adds Vivekananda's view that Vyasa was probably a tradition or group, since one person could not write so much. Many scholars see 'Vyasa' as a title for a line of compilers.

The three starting texts of Vedanta: the principal Upanishads (about eight to ten, such as Brihadaranyaka, Chandogya, Shvetashvatara, Katha, Kena, Isha), the Gita and the Brahma Sutra. A Vedanta philosopher is one who reads all three together and writes a Bhashya. The Gita is in easy language; the Upanishads are in older, harder Sanskrit.

A Rigveda line: 'the truth is one; the wise call it by many names'. The early Vedas show confusion between many gods ('to which god shall we offer?'), and the answer reached was that all paths are one path. It is the root of Vedanta's single Brahman.
'Not this, not this': the Upanishads' way of speaking of Brahman, which no description can hold. It is the nirguna view (God without attributes) that later returns in Kabir and Nanak.
Sage credited with the Vaisheshika Sutra; the atomic view of matter is linked to him.
Sage credited with the Mimamsa Sutra, the school the speaker calls the most important in Indian philosophy for its ritual and interpretive work.
Author of the Yoga Sutra; Yoga is paired with Samkhya in the six-school scheme.

Astika and Nastika can mean (1) believes in God, (2) believes in the afterlife, or (3) accepts the Vedas as proof. The speaker uses the third, the only one that sorts the schools cleanly: Nyaya believes God made the Vedas, Mimamsa says no one made them, Samkhya needs no creator, yet all are Astika.

Samkhya's three qualities that make up nature. Sattva: calm, light food, reading, humility. Rajas: energy, ambition, haste. Tamas: heaviness, sleep, inertia. Everyone has all three in different mixes, and nature, which becomes the world, is formed from them. Samkhya treats this world as real.

Earth, water, fire, air and space (kshiti, jal, pavak, samir, gagan), the Panchamahabhuta. Charvaka accepts only four, because you can feel earth, water, fire and air but cannot perceive pure space. The speaker notes that Tulsidas lists the same five in the Ramcharitmanas.

Most Indian schools say yes. Only three sects say it is not real but a phenomenon: Advaita Vedanta, and two Mahayana schools, Shunyavada (Nagarjuna) and Vijnanavada or Yogachara (Asanga and Vasubandhu). The speaker adds that Neo-Vedanta had to insist the world is real, or freedom and nationalism would mean nothing.

Great Buddhist centre in Bihar, linked in the lecture with Nagarjuna as its head and the brothers Asanga and Vasubandhu as teachers, all 'sitting together'. Historians date Nalanda's institutional flowering to the 5th century CE and later, so these three were not contemporaries there; the tradition connects them in memory.

The speaker's test: look at the end, not the start. Indian schools begin with suffering but end with liberation, so they are not pessimistic; Schopenhauer ends in despair. He adds that the line 'it is best never to have been born' is not advice to act on.

Judaism, Christianity and Islam all hold a soul (Islam calls it ruh), but the speaker says it is not eternal by nature: God can destroy it, and a soul sent to hell is destroyed, whereas the Indian soul is indestructible. Many theologians would say instead that souls endure, even in hell; the view of destruction is held by a minority.

In Genesis, Adam and Eve sinned in the garden of Eden and were sent to earth. The speaker says the Semitic aim is to return to God's heaven, so the goal lies in another world. In India the goal is escape from the cycle of birth and death; heaven appears only lightly (early Mimamsa, Vaikuntha in Vaishnavism).

In the Christian account Jesus is the Son of God (Father, Son, Holy Spirit), and he chose the cross to take on the sins of humanity. The speaker sees it as a transfer of karma, which Hinduism does not allow and the Mahayana does. Islam does not hold the Trinity or the crucifixion.

The Abrahamic belief that the dead are buried and on the day of judgment the same body regains consciousness, as Jesus did on Easter after Good Friday. The speaker contrasts it with reincarnation, which moves to a new body, and says in these faiths there is one life only.
The Jewish idea of rebirth of souls, taught in mystical Judaism. The speaker mentions a view that Moses returns in every generation.

Italian philosopher and scientist who taught rebirth, that the universe has countless suns, and that God is in the world. The Church imprisoned him for seven years and burned him at Rome in 1600. The speaker offers him as a martyr to free thought beside Socrates.

University of Virginia psychiatrist who spent about 40 years studying children who said they recalled past lives; wrote Twenty Cases Suggestive of Reincarnation and a study of birthmarks. He tried to disprove the claims and found about twenty cases he could not explain. The speaker says nothing is proved; mainstream science does not accept the work.

After the 1934 earthquake in Bihar Gandhi wrote that it was punishment for untouchability. He meant to move Hindu society, and later said he had written thoughtfully, not casually. The speaker says it fails: karma gives fruit only to the doer, yet upper-caste people died too. His advice: do not explain every accident through karma.

Critics say karma and rebirth justify caste, poverty and disability, and keep people in place. The speaker says one may take comfort in the idea, but no one can prove a given illness is a past deed, so it is a matter of belief.

Asked whether we are getting better or worse, the speaker says both: more civilised, wealthy and equal, yet nuclear and chemical weapons and ecological harm. On purpose, some think we are an accident and others that God sent us with one. Believing in purpose, he says, makes people happier, whether or not it is true.

A charge the speaker concedes in part. Charvaka, Jainism and Buddhism arose against elite ritual; learned women in the Upanishads and thinkers such as Osho and Ambedkar did not come from it. Work on the voices of oppressed classes is still new.

Philosophy and science grow where religious and philosophical debate is free. The speaker praises India's rich tradition of debate and says killings over religious difference were rare compared with the West (Socrates, Bruno).

nodes.l: Religion and philosophy: India and the West
nodes.d: In India nine schools are tied to a faith: Jain, Buddhist, six Astika, later Sikh. Their shared aim is freedom from suffering, so Indian philosophy is applied rather than academic. In Greece, philosophy and religion ran apart; Christian thinkers such as Augustine and Aquinas are exceptions.
Guru Nanak's opening statement of one formless supreme power, close to the nirguna God of Kabir.
Founded by Dayananda Saraswati in 1875 on ten principles. It stresses reasoned argument, rejects caste, supports gender equality and girls' education, and calls for a return to the Vedas.
A movement from England and the US that also worked in India. Annie Besant, one of its leaders, found the young Jiddu Krishnamurti and raised him.
British thinker in the Theosophical Society who worked in India. She took charge of Krishnamurti after a custody fight with his father.
The speaker's only medieval woman philosopher: a Bhakti poet-devotee of Krishna.
The speaker names her as a modern woman philosopher among eight to ten; the transcript does not say which Mahadevi, though Mahadevi Varma is the likely one.
Wife of Yajnavalkya; her dialogue with him in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad shows ideas of the self developing.
Scholar named in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, where she questions Yajnavalkya.
Wife of sage Agastya; the speaker places her in the Upanishads, but scholars know her from a Rigvedic hymn.
A woman seer; the speaker says she appears in the Upanishads, but she is a Rigvedic seer.

The speaker names Bhartiya Darshan ki Rooprekha by Harendra Prasad Sinha and, in English, A Critical Survey of Indian Philosophy by Chandradhar Sharma, both from Motilal Banarsidass, and says the next class turns to Charvaka.

The speaker says the Buddha was not a philosopher by nature but used philosophy to end suffering, as Gandhi, Ambedkar and Vivekananda did. Gandhi, he says, borrowed from Jainism, Christianity, the Gita and Ruskin's Unto This Last and said there is no 'Gandhism'. Shankara, Nagarjuna and Kant are the pure philosophers.

The speaker's retelling of a story, with no source given: a man asks the Buddha how to be happy, and is told to drop ego and lust, since happiness is what remains when the wrapping is removed. Treat it as an illustration, not a quotation.

Four about the world being eternal or not, four about its being finite or not, two on whether soul and body are the same, and four on whether the Tathagata exists after death. The speaker says 10, 12, 14 and 16 are all counted, and takes 14 as the best attested. Each of the four-part sets runs through the four logical corners.

Something lasting through all time (as the universe, or God as many believe) versus something beyond time (a mathematical truth such as 2 × 3 = 6). The question put to the Buddha, whether the world is eternal, concerns the first sense.

Kant's term for a question where equally weighty arguments can be given on both sides, so reason cannot settle it. The speaker gives it as one reason the Buddha kept silent on the world's limits, God and the soul.

In the Vaishnava story, Vishnu killed the demon on the doorstep, neither inside nor outside the house. The speaker uses it to show a fifth way of answering 'inside or outside?': both, and neither. It illustrates the four-cornered logic in a familiar story.

The speaker says the observable universe is about 13 billion light-years across and that nobody knows if it is finite; he also notes a video-game universe that loops would have no end. Cosmologists put the observable radius at roughly 46 billion light-years, because space expanded while light travelled. Whether the whole universe is finite is unknown.

The fat, smiling figure is not Gautama but Budai (Hotei in Japan), a Chinese monk of about the 10th century linked with Maitreya, the Buddha to come. The speaker notes that Gautama himself did not laugh in this way.

The Four Truths follow a doctor's order: the symptom (suffering), the cause (ignorance), the cure (Nirvana) and the treatment (the Eightfold Path). The speaker says 'Mahavaidya', the great physician, is an epithet of the Buddha. A similar four-part scheme is found in the Yoga Sutra.

nodes.l: Forward and reverse reading of the chain
nodes.d: The twelve links are given forward (ignorance to old age and death) and backward. A doctor starts with today's cough and works back to the first cigarette; the Buddha, seeking the root of suffering, likewise traced it back from old age and death to ignorance.
The Wheel of Becoming (Bhavachakra, Dharmachakra): a chain from ignorance to old age and death, each link arising in dependence on the one before. Cutting it ends suffering.
The impressions of past action carried in consciousness: the unsettled balance of karma. Also one of the five aggregates.
Consciousness as a flow, like an electric current rather than a thing. It carries the impressions of karma into the next birth. Also one of the five aggregates.
The mind-body organism that arises when consciousness needs a body.
The five outer senses and the mind as the inner sense. Without them there would be no contact.
The meeting of an organism and an object through the senses. If the two never met, as an animal never meets a taste it has no sense for, no craving would arise.
The pleasant, unpleasant or neutral feeling that follows contact. Also one of the five aggregates.
Wanting more of what felt pleasant. The speaker's example: someone who has never tasted a food will not feel deprived of it.
Holding on to worldly pleasure. The same word means the material cause, the clay of a pot, in other schools.
The tendency to be born again, which comes from karma left unsettled at death.
Birth, which makes all later suffering possible. The speaker says that for those never born there would be none, though he adds this is a philosophy class and not a biology class.
The symptom: old age, disease, death and, in the lecture's reading, all sorrow.

Ignorance means taking the impermanent for permanent, suffering for happiness and the non-self for the self (in this lecture, the body for 'I'). The speaker's example is a friend taken for a lifelong one.

What we call a person is a bundle of five: body (rupa), feeling (vedana), perception (sanjna), karmic impressions (samskara) and consciousness (vijnana). Remove them and nothing remains to be called a self. The transcript garbles the Pali names, so the standard list is used.
The physical form: limbs, organs, atoms. Each part is itself a collection of smaller parts, like a chariot.
Knowledge and recognition: what a person has seen and learned and remembers.

How a person at 2, 20 and 50 can be the same when the body and mind have changed. The speaker says the Upanishads answer with an unchanging self; the Buddha answers with the five aggregates and a continuous stream.

Indo-Greek king of the 2nd century BCE with a capital at Sagala (Sialkot), educated in Greek dialogue and well beaten by debate. He asked Nagasena how rebirth can occur without a soul. The record is the Milindapanha.
Buddhist monk of the Theravada line who debated Milinda; the Pali Milindapanha preserves it. The speaker stresses he is not Nagarjuna, who came about three centuries later in the South.

Nagasena asked the king if his chariot was the horses, the platform, the wheels, the axle, the pole, the flag or the seat. It was none, and the name is a label for their collection. So with a person: 'Nagasena' is only a name for the aggregates.

Greek rulers in north-west India after Alexander. Menander, who met Buddhist teachers, lived about the 2nd century BCE. Greek thought was then dialogical (Socrates, Plato) and Indian thought full of public debate.

Ashoka (3rd century BCE) made Buddhism a state patron and sent it to Sri Lanka and beyond. The lecture's 'two years after the death of the Buddha' is a garble; he came about two centuries later. Councils are counted at Rajagriha, Vaishali, Pataliputra under Ashoka and later in Kashmir.

Nothing is unchanging. Even if something lasts a long time, like the sun, its properties change, so it is not eternal in the Buddha's strict sense. Everything that depends on something else was once absent, so it cannot be permanent.

Later Buddhists, led by the Sthaviras, sharpened impermanence into momentariness: all real things change at every instant. The speaker's pictures: a child grown beyond recognition, a film of 24 frames a second, the river that cannot be entered twice. The claim that all body cells renew every seven years is a popular myth; renewal rates differ by tissue.
Every object and person is a collection of parts, and the parts are themselves collections. The transcript renders this as 'federalism'.
Inside every collection, momentary things arise and pass, each handing on to the next. A river, a flame and a person are each such a stream. The transcript renders this as 'childism'.

Later Buddhists said what is real is what can bring about an effect. A seed becomes a tree through stages, so it must change; something unchanging could produce nothing. Arthakriyakaritva is the technical term.

Advaita: what can never be sublated in past, present or future. Jain: what has arising, passing and persistence together. Buddhist: what can produce an effect. The speaker uses them to show why schools disagree about whether the world is real.

If everything lasts only a moment, how can someone recall, recognise a face or reap an old deed? The speaker's answer: each moment passes on nearly all of its content to the next, like data restored from a cloud backup, so continuity of karma and memory is kept.
The older monks who held to the original rules. They gave the Theravada school, and, through later development, Sarvastivada. The speaker calls them closest to the Buddha.
The larger, younger group who wanted change, whom the speaker links to the roots of the Mahayana.

If all is momentary, Nirvana cannot be lasting; if Nirvana is permanent, it would need a permanent cause, and a cause must be of the same kind as its effect. Buddhists found no tidy answer. The Theravada response was to treat Nirvana as outside the chain of dependent origination.
Things that fall outside dependent origination. In the early schools Nirvana is the first, with space as another. This is how Theravada keeps Nirvana permanent without an eternal soul.

nodes.l: Vedanta's charge: the Buddha kept the self
nodes.d: Upanishadic thinkers claim that by accepting a lasting Nirvana and a stream that carries karma, the Buddha did what the Atman does and did not truly escape the Upanishads. The speaker says the Buddhists answer that personal identity, karma and memory need no soul, but Nirvana was hardest.

Consciousness carries the unfinished balance of karma. At death, a body ends but the stream looks for a new body, as one lamp lights another; the flame is similar but not the same. Memory is mostly lost, though some say it persists in hidden form.

nodes.l: Indian views of the soul compared
nodes.d: Charvaka: only the living body. Nyaya and Vaisheshika: a substance whose consciousness is accidental, appearing with the body and gone at Moksha; Mimamsa similarly. Jain and Vaishnava Vedanta: consciousness is essential. Samkhya-Yoga: soul and consciousness are the same. Advaita: Atman is Brahman. Buddhism: no soul, only a stream.
The effect already exists in the cause. The speaker's picture: a sculptor says he did not make the statue, he removed what covered it. Held by Samkhya, Yoga and Vaishnava Vedanta.
The effect is something new and does not exist beforehand in the cause. The speaker lists Nyaya and Vaisheshika; Jainism takes a partly different view.
In Advaita, the effect is only an appearance of the cause, as a world seems real over Brahman.

The Charvaka view: the four elements combine by their own nature, with no God to mix them, and different ratios give humans, goats and birds. It is a mechanical, non-purposive account, close to Democritus' atoms. The speaker adds that the school only guessed here, since nobody saw the elements combine. The Buddha rejected it as strongly as he rejected a supernatural cause.
Greek thinker who classified everything. Of his four causes the speaker names the material (what it is made of) and the formal (its shape); he also named an efficient and a final cause.

Held causation as a fixed law: knowing all factors, one could know past and future. The speaker says he saw the ordered world as the work of a mathematician God; the transcript is garbled on this point.

Einstein held that God does not play dice; Hawking replied that God does play and sometimes hides the dice. Modern physics speaks of probability: a cause raises the chance of an effect without fixing it. Heisenberg stands behind the shift.
20th-century British humanist and Nobel winner, who like Hume treated causation as a habit of mind, and a sceptical agnostic about God.

17th-century empiricist: the mind begins like a blank sheet and all knowledge comes from experience. The speaker calls this tabula rasa; the Latin phrase is older than Locke, who wrote of 'white paper'. Locke and Berkeley still kept God and the soul.
American psychologist who described the self as a stream of consciousness, a phrase the speaker says matches the Buddha and later became a style in the novel. Also a founder of pragmatism.
French thinker (the transcript says 'Henry Burgess') who held that reality is ceaseless change. The speaker places him with those who echo the Buddha's flow.

In philosophy, theism means belief in a God who makes the world, keeps it going and ends it. In India the three tasks may be split among Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, and creation repeats in cycles; the Semitic faiths hold one God, and no cycle.

Omnipotent (all-powerful), omnipresent (everywhere), omniscient (all-knowing) and omnibenevolent (all-good). The speaker says each is hotly debated: if God is everywhere, he is also in what is dirty; if all-good and all-powerful, why is there evil?

nodes.l: Where the Indian schools stand on God
nodes.d: Five of nine do not accept God: Charvaka, Jain, Buddhist, Samkhya and Mimamsa. Yoga admits God only as an aid to meditation. Nyaya-Vaisheshika has God start the motion of atoms. Advaita holds God on the practical level only and Brahman beyond. Vaishnava Vedanta alone holds God in the full sense, and holds him central.
Yoga accepts God as an aid, not a goal: a closed-eye meditator needs something to fix the mind on. 'Ishvara-pranidhana' (surrender to God) is that device, so God is not important in its path.

Dogmatic atheism says one knows there is no God; sceptical atheism says one doubts and does not claim; agnosticism says God lies beyond our knowing, and may be soft (live as if) or hard. The speaker calls the first the least wise, because no one can prove it.

Not moral is not the same as immoral: sleepwalking harm is non-moral. By that logic the Buddha was a non-theist: God was not his question and he refused to build an idol. Jainism is called trans-theist, since each soul may become a god. The speaker adds that a smile was his answer to 'Is there a God?'.

If God is all-powerful and all-good, why are there tsunamis, quakes and child deaths? Semitic thinkers have 50 answers; Buddhists asked it of Vaishnava Vedanta. The speaker cites Gandhi's remark on the Bihar quake as a moral answer that fails the logic test.

nodes.l: Why would a perfect God create?
nodes.d: A perfect being lacks nothing and so wants nothing; without desire, no purpose. The speaker says no philosopher has answered why such a being made the world; 'lila' (play) is the usual Indian reply and 'God's wisdom' the Western.
Making God in human shape. The speaker quotes the Greek Xenophanes: if horses could write, their gods would be horses. Some say God made man; others, that man made God.

The speaker says people need a cause for everything and a watcher over injustice, so belief brings comfort whatever its truth. He says no religion is older than about 5,000 years; archaeology (Gobekli Tepe, about 9500 BCE) points to ritual far earlier. He also gives Homo sapiens as about 3 million years; it is about 300,000.
Austrian psychologist and an atheist, who said Marx had dropped God only to build a new one.

German thinker and an atheist. The speaker, who taught under a Marxist influence, says Marxism has the shape of a religion: Marx and Engels as prophets, Das Kapital as scripture, communism as heaven, revolution as the path. Radhakrishnan and Freud said the same.

German philosopher, a priest's son, who wrote against Christianity (The Antichrist), spoke of the will to power and the superman, and called Christian morality 'slave morality'. He thought Buddhism far more realistic than Christianity yet still nihilistic. Later militarists misused him.
Greek playwright whose Oedipus at Colonus says the best is never to be born; the next best is to die soon after birth. The speaker notes the line was made famous by Schopenhauer.
Greek philosopher who lived in a tub and, when Alexander offered him a favour, asked him to move out of his sunlight. The speaker uses him to show that happiness need not be striven for.

nodes.l: Judge a thinker by his mature view
nodes.d: A thinker who rejects his early books should be judged on his last, as with the early and later Marx. The speaker uses this to defend the Buddha: his last view is that suffering can end.

The charge started with Schopenhauer and Nietzsche and was echoed by Ambedkar. The speaker's replies: some thinkers see joy, but ruin a party by finding sorrow in it, which is a matter of temperament; and he who points out the way to end suffering cannot be called hopeless. He advises avoiding the label.

To give Buddhism a god, the Mahayana taught three forms: the earthly body (Gautama who walked in Kapilavastu), a heavenly body of bliss (such as Amitabha, who lives in a paradise and does not come to earth) and the dharma-body, an unnameable ultimate akin to Shankara's Brahman. Shunyavada calls it shunya; the speaker says Yogachara uses another term.

nodes.l: The Buddha as avatar of Vishnu
nodes.d: The Puranas (about the 4th–8th century) named the Buddha, and sometimes Mahavira, as an avatar of Vishnu, in a friendly reading (to stop animal sacrifice) or a hostile one (to lure the unruly away). The speaker says it reconciled a strong rival and blurred its separate identity.
In the Puranic period (about the 4th–8th century) the Buddha becomes the ninth avatar. The speaker names the Vishnu, Agni and Skanda Puranas.

12th-century poet of the Gita Govinda, whose Dashavatara hymn praises the Buddha as the ninth avatar in friendly terms ('Keshava, who took the Buddha's body'). The speaker adds that the well-known 'Om Jai Jagdish Hare' aarti is a 19th-century work by Shraddha Ram Phillauri and does not mention the Buddha.
Bakhtiyar Khilji's army sacked Nalanda about 1200 CE, and Buddhism in India weakened sharply thereafter, though it persisted in places. It had been strong from Ashoka's time through the Guptas.

A Puranic story the speaker retells: to weaken the demons, the gods' teacher Brihaspati made a pleasure-loving philosophy that would lure them. The speaker says it is hard to say how true it is. It is a tale told about Charvaka, not Charvaka's own account.

Negative: freedom from pain only, held by Samkhya, Yoga and the early (Hinayana) Buddhists. Positive: bliss, held by Advaita, Vaishnava Vedanta and Mahayana; the Jain soul has infinite knowledge, bliss and power. Nyaya-Vaisheshika's soul loses consciousness and becomes like a stone, which the speaker says no one would choose.

A line the speaker cites from the Pali tradition, 'Nirvana is the highest happiness', which Mahayana readers take as positive. Scholars such as Oldenberg, he says, read early Buddhism as only negative; the verse (in the Dhammapada) tells against that.
Jivanmukti: Samkhya-Yoga, Advaita, Buddhism and Jainism allow liberation before death. Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa and all Vaishnava schools say liberation comes only at death.

Buddhists say Sopadhishesha Nirvana when a liberated person still lives, Nirupadhishesha at death (Parinirvana); 'Mahaparinirvana' is reserved for the Buddha. Navayana followers honour Ambedkar's death on 6 December as Mahaparinirvan Diwas.

At liberation all stored (sanchita) karma is burned; the part already bearing fruit (prarabdha) must run out, like a fan that spins on after the switch is off or a potter's wheel after he stops. Then the body falls and there is no rebirth.
A liberated person acts, but without desire or hate, so the act leaves no new karma, like a roasted seed that cannot sprout. Samkhya, Yoga, Vedanta and Buddhism are said to agree.
Knowledge is the main path in Advaita, Samkhya, Jainism and Buddhism; devotion in Vaishnava Vedanta; the eight limbs of yoga in Yoga; ritual action in Mimamsa. Most schools mix them.
Navadha bhakti: hearing, singing, remembering, serving the feet, worship, bowing, serving as a servant, friendship and self-surrender.
Yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana and samadhi. The last stage, asamprajnata samadhi, is where liberation is said to come.
Right faith, right knowledge and right conduct together make the path. The speaker pairs them with the Buddha's three groups: wisdom, conduct and meditation.
The first two limbs: right view and right resolve. They set the mind in order.
The limbs of behaviour: speech, action and livelihood (the canon), with effort added in the lecture's grouping.
The final limbs: effort, mindfulness and concentration, ending in Nirvana. The speaker links it with the 28 days (tradition says one night) of sitting before enlightenment.
Seeing the world truly: suffering where we see happiness, the impermanent as impermanent and oneself as no soul. The speaker says Vaishnavas would add that one then sees God in every particle.
Holding firmly to the true view when everyone calls you wrong.
Speak little, truthfully, kindly and without insult. The speaker cites the Sanskrit rule 'speak the truth, speak what is pleasant, do not speak a pleasant lie'.
Do good, help others, harm no one, and so remove negativity from one's behaviour.
Training the mind and senses and keeping the right ideas fresh so they do not slip. The speaker calls it practice, not morning exercise.
Constant remembering of what the right view shows. The transcript garbles this limb; the name is from the canon.
Deep stillness of mind, ending in Nirvana. The speaker says the first seven limbs are gathered and sunk into this last.

Jayarashi Bhatta's book, the first full text we have from this line, about 1,500 years after Ajita. It is a sceptic's attack on every claim to knowledge, perception included, so it does not match the neat 'perception only' formula; scholars debate whether it is Charvaka at all. The speaker says it is one of two friendly sources and dates it to the 9th century; most scholars say about the 8th.

A Sanskrit play by Krishna Mishra in which ideas appear as characters. The speaker calls it the only work written in favour of Charvaka; scholars read it as a Vaishnava allegory in which Charvaka appears as a character and loses.

'Collection of all the philosophies', attributed to Madhava, the Vidyaranya of the Vijayanagara court and Shringeri monastery. Its first chapter on Charvaka is where about 90% of the school's quotations come from, as the speaker says. Authorship is debated, and the account is written by a Vedantin who disagrees with it.

nodes.l: Knowing a school only through its critics
nodes.d: Charvaka's own books are lost, so we read them through Buddhist, Jain and Vedantic opponents. The speaker warns that critics seldom state an opponent's view at its best, 'a judge of others and a lawyer for himself', and says the opponents' arguments still show roughly what was said. The same lesson applies to any person judged only on a rival's account.
Indian scholar of philosophy (author of Outlines of Indian Philosophy) whom the speaker cites for the rule that we know very little of Charvaka and should give it the benefit of the doubt.
Radhakrishnan, as the speaker reports, argued that Charvaka forced other schools to defend their claims and so saved Indian philosophy from dogmatism, as Hume's doubt did in the West.
Not named in the lecture; added for context. Historian of Indian materialism whose Lokayata (1959) gathered the scattered evidence for the school and its links to everyday life.

(1) From the root 'to chew': those who chew up morals, or, as a hostile pun, chew meat; (2) charu + vak, 'sweet speech', for their persuasive talk; (3) a man called Charvaka whose followers took his name. Nobody knows. A demon Charvaka also appears in the Mahabharata, a different figure, which hostile writers used to colour the name.

'Found only in the world (loka)': the school says nothing exists beyond this world, and some add that the name also fits a view popular among ordinary people. Kautilya's Arthashastra lists Lokayata with Samkhya and Yoga as a school of reasoning, so it was a recognised school, not just a joke.

Author of the Kamasutra, who the speaker suggests may be the same as Brihaspati in the Charvaka line. Standard dating puts him about the 3rd century CE; the Kamasutra is about arts of pleasure, not a Charvaka text, and the Nyaya commentator Vatsyayana is another person.

In public memory the school is a drunkard's philosophy. The speaker says this is a caricature built on two verses (borrow and drink ghee; drink, fall, rise, drink again). His point: look at the conditions of the country, put yourself there, and the thinker's words start to make sense.

Pioneer of modern Hindi literature (1850–85). The speaker cites a comic song about drink in his satirical play on India's wretched state (Bharat Durdasha) as one place the Charvaka image of drunkenness survives.

Poet of Madhushala, whose wine, cup and tavern are symbols for spiritual intoxication. The speaker says the verse about breaking the quarrel between temple and mosque by sitting everyone in the tavern is a call to unity, not to drinking.
Hindi poet whose Kurukshetra the speaker quotes for the Charvaka thought: forget the world beyond and make this world beautiful.
Jaishankar Prasad's epic poem, which the speaker reads as showing the Deva civilization ruined by pleasure alone, a literary rebuttal to the Charvaka ideal.

Pleasure is the highest good. The speaker says Charvaka is the only Indian school that says so, in a world where eight of nine schools aim at Moksha. He stresses that it speaks of the individual's pleasure, not society's. His later Gita lecture raises the paradox of hedonism: those who aim only at happiness often miss it.

Do pleasures differ only in intensity, or also in kind?
