The speaker says Charvaka counted only intensity, so the joy of helping and the pleasure of scratching an itch count alike, as Bentham said in 19th-century Britain. Later 'cultured' Charvakas, he says, admitted higher pleasures. J. S. Mill, whom the lecture does not name, is the Western voice who argued the same.
British utilitarian (1748–1832) who held that only the amount of pleasure matters, not its kind. The speaker compares this to Charvaka.
Greek hedonist (about 435–356 BCE) whom the speaker names as saying much the same as Charvaka. The speaker also cites D. H. Lawrence (the transcript says 'D.S.') as a modern echo.
Not named in the lecture; added for contrast. His 'pleasure' meant calm of mind and simple living, very unlike the feast the Charvaka caricature suggests.

Later writers divide the school into the dhurta (rogue) and the susikshita (well-schooled) types. The speaker's 'educated Charvakas' belong here (his reference to the Upanishads is a garble): they allowed higher pleasures and worldly virtue.

The best-known Charvaka maxim, recorded in the Sarvadarshanasangraha: while life lasts, live happily; when the body is ash, how can it return? 'Ghee' is clarified butter, though the speaker reads it as drink. Its point is that there is no rebirth, so the pleasure must be taken now.
Dharma (duty), artha (wealth), kama (pleasure), Moksha (liberation). The speaker says Charvaka keeps only kama (some records keep artha as its means). Eight of the nine schools put Moksha highest.
Charvaka's answer to Moksha: apavarga, the end of the cycle, is simply death, with nothing after. Heaven is pleasure and hell is pain, here and now.
The speaker's praise: the only Indian school that asks whether making this life good could be enough. He calls it 'secular' in the sense of 'of this world', not in the sense of church and state.

Sarvadarshanasangraha reports Charvaka verses mocking ritual: the Vedas were made by buffoons, knaves and demons; if shraddha offerings feed the dead, feed travellers at home; if sacrificed animals go to heaven, sacrifice your parents. The speaker calls religion a 'mental illness' in their words and sets Kabir beside it. The Buddha's stand on sacrifice was milder.
All knowledge comes from experience. The speaker names Locke, Berkeley and Hume as Western supporters. Berkeley held that matter does not exist, the opposite of Charvaka's materialism.
18th-century Irish empiricist and idealist: to be is to be perceived, so there is no matter outside mind. The speaker lists him among empiricists.
Direct knowledge through the five senses, plus the mind for pleasure and pain. Charvaka's only valid source.
Seeing a wet road and concluding it rained. Charvaka said inference cannot be trusted.
Knowledge from a trusted person, as in trusting a doctor's diagnosis. Charvaka rejected it, which meant rejecting the Vedas as proof.
Learning about an unseen thing from a description and its likeness to a known one, as in recognising an elephant.
Knowledge by implication: a man fat in daylight who never eats by day must eat by night.
Knowing that something is absent, as in seeing that a person is not in the room.

Charvaka one; Buddhists and Vaisheshika two; Samkhya and Yoga three; Nyaya four; Prabhakara Mimamsa five; Bhatta Mimamsa and Advaita Vedanta six. The lecture lumps Vedanta with the three-source schools; that fits Vishishtadvaita but not Advaita.

The basis of inference: smoke always goes with fire. Charvaka asked how anyone can see every case, so no universal link is ever established; Nyaya replied with inference by long experience and by testing counter-cases.

Classic reply by Nyaya, Buddhists and Jains: to argue with an opponent, you must infer his mind from his words, so denying inference uses it. The speaker's own critique is different: perception alone cannot run a life (you would not take an umbrella or leave a burning house).

Jaundice turns white to yellow, double vision doubles, a moving train makes the platform move, the earth looks flat and the sun looks to rise. Some sounds, such as a dog whistle, are out of our range. The speaker uses all this to show senses are limited, and Charvaka's claim is overreaching.

Thoughts, emotions and atoms cannot be seen, and no one has seen the galaxies or a nuclear weapon at first hand. The speaker's reply: God or soul may be unproven, but unseen is not the same as non-existent.

The fifth element. Space cannot be touched, seen or smelt; you see objects in space, not space. So Charvaka dropped it, as the speaker says Ajita (whom he runs together with Pakudha) and Empedocles also kept four.

Greek philosopher (5th c. BCE) who taught four 'roots': earth, air, fire, water, mixed and parted by Love and Strife. The speaker pairs him with Pakudha Kaccayana, though the Pali texts give Pakudha seven elements and Ajita four.
Greek atomist (5th c. BCE) who taught that all things are atoms moving in void, with no purpose or mind behind them.
Early Greek thinker (6th c. BCE) who made air the first principle.
Greek thinker (about 500 BCE) who taught that what is cannot change or perish.
The speaker lists Thales (water), Anaximenes (air), Heraclitus (fire) and Parmenides (being) as many Western matter-thinkers; India, he says, has one clear school of materialists.
The world as a self-running process with no designer or purpose; the speaker contrasts it with creationism, which holds God made it for a purpose.

From the Sarvadarshanasangraha: grain and yeast are not intoxicating, but fermented they are; leaf, nut and lime are not red, but chewed they colour the lips. So consciousness appears when elements combine. The speaker says that using analogies is weak philosophy, though sometimes needed; critics note fermentation needs a further cause, and an analogy proves nothing.

A claim that the soul weighs 21 grams. The speaker rejects it, noting that a thought does not weigh more because you read a book. It traces to Duncan MacDougall's 1907 experiment on six dying patients, which was never reproduced.

Not named in the lecture. David Chalmers' phrase (1995) for why physical processes should come with felt experience; the speaker's own form of it is that 'iron cannot make mind', as cotton cannot make ice.
Indian communist-turned-radical-humanist (1887–1954). The speaker names him, with Marx in the West, among modern materialists.

Chemistry now lists 118 elements, of which about 90-odd occur in nature and the rest are made in labs. The speaker's point: ancient lists were hypotheses, philosophy first put the question, and nothing in knowledge is wasted.

Greek sophist (5th c. BCE) who argued nothing exists, or if it does it cannot be known or told. The speaker (name garbled in the transcript) compares this with Sanjaya's scepticism, about a century earlier.

Medieval writers often speak of three Vedas (trayi), treating the Atharvaveda as partly repeating the rest. The speaker says that when Charvaka attacks 'the three Vedas' it is not rejecting only three.

The speaker's contrast: the Vedas look outward, with many gods, prayers for cattle and long life, heaven and ritual; the Upanishads look inward, with karma, rebirth and Moksha, and send people into the forest. Other world religions also began with many gods tied to sun, fire and water.

The speaker says the best people of society leave it, and quotes this as a remark made by Vivekananda in America (I cannot confirm the source). He sees it as a reason for the restlessness of the 6th century that fed the Shramana movement.

The speaker's reply to a question: the sociology of religion explains its social use, such as meeting people, shared meals and company for the elderly and for women who rarely go out. It does not answer intellectual questions; philosophy of religion does.
Not named in the lecture; the transcript has garbled names at this point and probably means Durkheim and Weber. French founder of sociology, who read religion as the way a society holds together.
German sociologist; see the note on Durkheim. The lecture names Marx outright and two garbled names.

nodes.l: Why we do not act on what we know
nodes.d: Asked why knowledge of the right thing does not become action, the speaker answers: conscience and desire pull against each other and desire often wins; being moral takes effort, being weak does not; religion supports habit, while a thinking person must weigh every case. The Greeks called the gap akrasia.

Jains and Buddhists meditate, Vedic people perform yajna for heaven, but Charvaka, wanting nothing beyond this life, had no method of spiritual practice. The speaker separates it from Vajrayana, which seems alike in boldness but is a disciplined Buddhist path.

The speaker accepts Osho's view that the school's books were destroyed, and mentions Khilji's burning of Nalanda in the same breath. Historians have no evidence of a campaign against Charvaka books; neglect, lack of institutions and scribal choice may explain the loss as well.

The speaker: it had no monastery, no practice and no appeal of renunciation, so it could not become an institution. Buddhism fled abroad (Japan, Korea, China, Sri Lanka) and Jainism survives with about 40 lakh believers in India. Today, he says, most people live like Charvakas without the name.

nodes.l: Doubt as the root of science
nodes.d: Osho's claim, as the speaker retells it, that India would have had more scientists if Charvaka had survived. The speaker agrees history turns on accidents and that doubt is part of science's ethos; he does not claim to know what would have followed.

The speaker's roadmap for the Gita's ethics: Nishkama Karma Yoga, Sthitaprajna (the steady-minded), Lokasangraha (holding the world together) and avatarism. He advises exam candidates to name all four. This transcript develops only the first, plus Swadharma, and stops before the other three, so those nodes carry no lecture detail.

Named in the roadmap but not covered in the transcript. In the Gita (chapter 2, about verses 54–72) the term describes a person whose mind stays level in pleasure and pain; the detail here is from standard sources, not the lecture.

Named in the roadmap but not covered in the transcript. In the Gita (3.20 and 3.25) it means acting for the good of the world so that society holds together; the detail is from standard sources, not the lecture.

The speaker promises to explain its ethical side at the end, but the transcript stops before it. In the Gita (4.7–8) Krishna says he takes birth whenever right declines; the verse reference is from standard sources, not the lecture.

The Gita's best-known teaching, as the speaker puts it: act fully, but do not cling to the result. He glosses 'nishkama' as free of desire or attachment, and stresses that the detachment is from the fruit, not from the work.

Added for context. The Gita's own phrases are anasakta karma (action without attachment) and phalatyaga (giving up the fruit); 'nishkama karma' is the standard later label. Gandhi called the teaching anasaktiyoga, and Tilak's reading is titled Karmayoga.

nodes.l: Gita 2.47: the right is to the action only
nodes.d: The speaker's central verse. Its four parts as he gives them: you have a right to action alone; never to its fruits; do not make the fruit your motive; and do not cling to inaction. 'You have only the right to do your duty, not to desire the fruit.'

nodes.l: Attach to the work, detach from the result
nodes.d: The speaker's reading: 'attachment' is clinging to the outcome, and the Gita asks you to put your whole self into the act while not being driven by what it will bring. He compares it to a popular Hindi film song on doing your work and leaving the reward.

nodes.l: Detachment is a matter of degree
nodes.d: The speaker answers the charge that the teaching is impractical. Thinking in all-or-nothing terms makes total detachment impossible, and he calls that one of the most basic fallacies in logic. People stand at points on a scale: a hungry baby cries only to get fed, while a student may study for pure interest. The closer you are to the detached end, he says, the steadier your life.

nodes.l: Enjoy the process, not the result
nodes.d: The speaker's example: some students read for love of the subject and are content whatever the exam brings, while those who want only the result are anxious. His advice for an interview is to treat it as a half hour with five senior people, a chance worth enjoying. He says real happiness belongs to those who enjoy the process.

The speaker uses the term to say that if you keep thinking about being happy you will not be, as with someone who cannot sleep because of thinking about sleep. Added for context: the phrase was made current by Henry Sidgwick (The Methods of Ethics, 1874); Mill noted something similar in his Autobiography.

nodes.l: The fruit is assured by the moral order
nodes.d: The speaker says detachment does not mean there is no fruit: there is a moral system in which you get what you deserve, if not now then in a later life, so you need not worry about it. Added for context: elsewhere the Gita also asks that actions be offered to Krishna (9.27).

What the Gita means by duty, the speaker says: not a general rule of morality but the duty fitted to one's own role and nature. A soldier should fight, a king should rule, and neither should compromise the duty given to him. He says this is the message in practice: live by your Swadharma and do not think about the fruit.

The speaker's most famous line on duty (Gita 3.35, repeated in 18.47): it is better to die in one's own duty than to follow another's, which brings fear. The standard text adds that one's own duty is better even when done imperfectly; the transcript omits that clause.

The Gita ties Swadharma to svabhava, one's basic nature (chapter 18). The speaker finds this comfortable in the case of the soldier or king, and says the problem begins only when the text says duty follows the Varna.

nodes.l: The Varna problem in the Gita
nodes.d: The speaker calls this the only real difficulty in its ethics. Some sociologists, he says, hold that every society needs a religious text to support its social order, and that the Gita did so for Varna; Ambedkar is its main critic on this. The speaker calls the text a grey area: it does not say Varna goes by birth.

nodes.l: Gita 4.13: four varnas by quality and action
nodes.d: Krishna says he made the four varnas by the distribution of guna and karma (quality and action). The speaker reads this as an aptitude-based scheme. The next lines of the verse, not quoted in the lecture, call Krishna the maker yet 'not the doer'.

The speaker's thought experiment: a Varna system could be open, letting a merchant's son who tests as a scholar become a Brahmin, and a person change role in their own life. He says that if the Gita's Varna was open it is defensible, and if birth-bound it should not be supported, and admits he is no historian. Historians note that most classical commentators read the verses as birth-based, while reformers such as Dayananda argued for merit.

The speaker argues that Krishna, raised in a family of cowherds, chose to be a strategist and charioteer, which would show that roles were open. Historians point out that the Mahabharata calls Krishna a Kshatriya of the Yadava line raised among cowherds, so the example proves less than the speaker suggests.

The speaker says Ambedkar wrote generally against the Gita. Added for context: in 'Krishna and His Gita' he argued that it defended the caste order and Brahmanical reaction against Buddhism; other scholars contest this reading.

nodes.l: Judging a system by its own time
nodes.d: The speaker's caution: every age has its limits, so condemning the past by today's standards is poor history. In 500 years people will judge us as harshly. The test he proposes is whether the system allowed movement, and he adds that he would write on the subject in an exam only if asked.

Added for context. The Gita opens with Arjuna, facing kin on the other side, refusing to fight. Krishna's reply that duty must be done without clinging to the result is what the lecture's ethics rests on.
Added for context. Nationalist leader (1856–1920) whose commentary Gita Rahasya, written in jail in Mandalay and published in 1915, read the Gita as a call to action rather than withdrawal.

Added for context. Kant held that an act is right when done from duty, whatever the outcome. The Gita's Swadharma differs: it fits duty to a person's role and nature, where Kant's duty applies to all alike.
